body:
## What copper theft looks like in 2026

Scrap copper sits near $4 per pound. A single substation hit yields hundreds of pounds of grounding wire, transformer windings, and bus bar. The street value of that haul is $1,500 to $4,000. The replacement and downtime cost to the utility is $80,000 to $300,000 — and that's before regulatory penalties for an outage.

The crime pattern is consistent. Suspects scout during daylight, return between 1am and 4am, cut through fencing or use a ladder over it, and work fast. Construction sites lose copper feeder wire from generators and panels. Telecom huts lose grounding bars. Oil and gas pads lose copper bonding straps. Abandoned buildings get stripped of wire and pipe in a single night.

Static surveillance cameras record the theft. They do not prevent it. The suspects have masks and a stolen vehicle. By the time the footage is reviewed, the copper is at a scrap yard 80 miles away.

## How VDS prevents copper theft

Mobile Surveillance Unit is built for this threat. Thermal imaging detects body heat through brush, fence cover, and low light — the visual camera misses the suspect, the thermal camera does not. Radar detects movement at the property line before a perimeter breach, giving the SOC 30 to 90 seconds of lead time.

AI VisionStream classifies the target. Person at the fence line at 2am, on foot, carrying tools — that is not a deer or a security false alarm. The rule fires, the alert hits a US SOC operator's screen, and the operator initiates live audio talk-down through the unit's speaker: "You are on private utility property. Law enforcement has been dispatched. Leave the area now."

In our case data, audio talk-down ends the incident before any wire is touched in the majority of cases. When it doesn't, the operator dispatches local police with a live video feed and exact GPS coordinates.

## Recommended VDS configuration

- **Mobile Surveillance Unit at the substation interior** — $2,200/mo. Thermal + radar + 4K visual + LPR + active deterrence. Solar-autonomous, no trenching, repositionable.
- **Mobile Surveillance Unit along the fence-line** — $1,800/mo per 500-foot run. Detects an approach before the suspect reaches the fence.
- **AI VisionStream rules** — person-at-fence-line, loitering, tool detection, after-hours zones.
- **24/7 US SOC** — <60s escalation, audio talk-down, LE dispatch, evidence preservation.

faq.a: Yes. Thermal imaging detects heat signatures through most non-metallic cover including brush, tarps, and chain-link. It is the single highest-value sensor for substation copper theft.

## What cargo theft looks like in 2026

CargoNet reported a sustained surge in strategic cargo theft through 2023 and 2024 — fictitious pickups, identity theft of legitimate carriers, double-brokered loads, and yard infiltrations. The top targets remain consistent: electronics, food and beverage, household goods, and apparel. A single full trailer can carry $100,000 to $500,000 in product. Some loads exceed $1 million.

The crime moves fast. A tractor with cloned DOT credentials backs into a dock, drops the legitimate trailer, hooks up the target, and pulls out — in under 15 minutes. Or a perimeter breach at 3am, a stolen yard tractor, and a high-value trailer is gone before the dispatcher notices. Recovery rates are below 25%. Insurance covers some of it; the customer relationship damage covers none of it.

Static cameras at the gate see the truck. They do not see that the trailer hookup at dock 14 at 2:47am was unauthorized. They do not alert anyone in time to stop it.

## How VDS prevents cargo theft

VDS treats the yard as a system. Mobile Surveillance Unit runs the fence-line — every approach to the perimeter triggers an alert before the breach. Mobile Surveillance Unit units at every vehicle entrance run LPR with 95%+ accuracy in under 3 seconds, logging every tractor and trailer plate against your authorized list.

AI VisionStream rules catch the patterns static cameras miss. Trailer-hookup detection during after-hours windows fires when a tractor docks without a corresponding dispatch record. Loitering rules alert on a vehicle parked at the property line for more than 4 minutes. The SOC operator pulls live video, verifies in seconds, and either talks the driver down through the on-unit speaker or dispatches law enforcement with plate, GPS, and direction of travel.

## What catalytic converter theft looks like in 2026

A 2008 Toyota Prius converter contains roughly 4-7 grams of platinum group metals. Black market price: $400 to $1,200. With rhodium back above $10,000 per ounce in 2026 after the 2024 dip, the economics of converter theft have returned. The cut itself takes 60 to 90 seconds with a battery-powered reciprocating saw. A two-person crew can hit 10 to 20 vehicles in a single overnight stop at a dealer lot, fleet yard, hotel parking deck, or hospital parking ramp.

The replacement cost to the vehicle owner runs $1,500 to $3,500 per converter. For a dealership, a single bad night means 15 inoperable vehicles, customer complaints, insurance claims, and a service department backlog. Hotels and hospitals face guest lawsuits over inadequate premises security. Fleet operators with 50+ vans face the math of which 30 converters they can replace this week.

Static cameras catch the silhouette of the cut. They don't stop it.

## How VDS prevents catalytic converter theft

The window to intervene is short — under 90 seconds per vehicle. VDS detection has to fire in seconds and response has to be immediate. Mobile Surveillance Unit units in the lot run dual-spectrum night vision and AI VisionStream rules tuned for crouching, loitering between vehicles, and unauthorized after-hours pedestrian movement. Thermal imaging is the unlock — a person crouched behind a vehicle is invisible to a standard PTZ at 2am but glows on thermal.

The moment the rule fires, the SOC operator has live video on screen. Live audio talk-down through the unit's speaker: "You are on camera, law enforcement has been dispatched, leave the lot immediately." In the majority of cases this ends the incident before the saw starts. LPR on the same unit captures the getaway vehicle plate, which is handed to the responding officers in real time.

## Recommended VDS configuration

- **Mobile Surveillance Unit units across the lot** — $1,500/mo each. HD PTZ + dual-spectrum night vision + AI analytics + LPR. One unit typically covers a 200-vehicle dealer row.
- **AI VisionStream rules** — crouching detection, after-hours pedestrian, loitering between vehicles, vehicle stopped on lot perimeter for >2 minutes.
- **24/7 US SOC** — live audio talk-down, plate capture handed to dispatched officers.
- **Optional Mobile Surveillance Unit** at lot perimeter for thermal long-range coverage on larger fleet yards.

## What illegal dumping looks like in 2026

Illegal dumping is a per-trip economic decision. A contractor with a truck of construction debris faces a $75 to $200 disposal fee at a licensed transfer station, or zero dollars if they pull into a quiet construction site, a vacant lot, or an alley dumpster at 11pm. The math favors dumping when the perceived enforcement risk is low.

The cost shifts to the property owner. Cleanup of a small dump runs $200 to $500. A truckload of mixed construction debris runs $1,200 to $2,000. Hazardous material — paint, solvents, tires, appliances — adds disposal cost and regulatory exposure. Municipal property managers carry insurance penalties for repeat incidents. Commercial real estate owners face tenant complaints and lease violations.

The pattern is repetitive. Once a site is identified as a "free" dump location, the same vehicles return. Without intervention, one incident becomes weekly incidents.

## How VDS prevents illegal dumping

The intervention is two-stage: deterrent and identification. Mobile Surveillance Unit at the site entrance runs LPR with 95%+ accuracy in under 3 seconds — every vehicle that enters is logged with timestamp, plate, and direction. AI VisionStream rules trigger on vehicles entering during off-hours, vehicles stopping for more than 4 minutes, and vehicles backing up to dumpsters or open ground.

The SOC operator pulls live video the moment a rule fires. Audio talk-down through the unit's speaker: "You are being recorded on private property. Your license plate has been logged and reported to local authorities. Leave the site now." In our case data, this ends the attempt in roughly 9 out of 10 cases before the load is dropped. When it doesn't, the LPR record and video are handed to local code enforcement or police for citation.

## What after-hours intrusion looks like in 2026

The crime window is consistent across construction sites, retail strip centers, auto dealerships, warehouses, and industrial yards: 10pm to 5am. Suspects scout during business hours, identify gaps in lighting and patrol coverage, and return when the site is empty. Tools, copper, equipment, vehicles, electronics — anything portable and valuable is on the table.

The conventional response options each fail differently. Static recorded video provides post-incident footage but no deterrent and no intervention. Guard services run $30 to $50 per hour, or $22,000 to $36,000 per month for 24/7 coverage at one site — and a single guard cannot watch a multi-acre property, gets fatigued, and creates its own liability exposure. Alarm systems with central station monitoring escalate slowly and generate enough false alarms that police response is deprioritized.

After-hours liability is rising in parallel — premises security litigation against property owners has expanded significantly over the past decade.

## How VDS prevents after-hours intrusion

VDS combines automated detection with human intervention. AI VisionStream runs time-of-day rules — after-hours zones arm automatically based on site schedule. The rule set includes person-on-site detection, vehicle loitering, fence-line breach, and perimeter approach. Thermal imaging on Mobile Surveillance Unit detects body heat in low light, through brush, and behind cover. Radar detects movement at the property line before a breach.

When a rule fires, the alert reaches a US SOC operator's console in seconds. The operator pulls live video, classifies the threat, and acts: live audio talk-down through the on-unit speaker, LE dispatch with GPS and direction of travel, evidence preservation. 97% false alarm reduction through AI pre-filtering means the alerts that reach a human are real.

Our Mid-Atlantic GC case study site saw a 73% reduction in theft incidents over 12 months, zero insurance claims, and $340,800 in avoided losses on a $28M project.

body:
## What vandalism looks like in 2026

Vandalism is rarely random. Construction sites get hit because they're empty after 6pm and the materials are tempting. Retail strip centers get tagged because the rear loading bay is unwatched. Schools get hit on weekends and breaks. Parks get hit overnight. The repair cost runs $500 for a graffiti cleanup, $1,500 to $5,000 for broken glass and signage, and $10,000+ for sabotage to equipment, HVAC condensers, or fire suppression systems.

The reputational cost is harder to quantify but real. A vandalized storefront signals neglect. A tagged construction site signals an unmonitored project to the entire neighborhood — and once a site is identified as soft, the pattern repeats. One incident becomes a cluster. A school with weekend graffiti loses parent confidence. A retail property with broken windows loses tenant interest.

Vandalism is a loitering crime. Suspects approach, assess the site, position themselves, and then act. That approach window — typically 30 seconds to 4 minutes — is where prevention happens.

## How VDS prevents vandalism

VDS targets the loiter window. AI VisionStream loitering detection rules fire when a person remains in a zone for more than a threshold (typically 60 to 120 seconds) during after-hours periods. Thermal imaging on Mobile Surveillance Unit detects the suspect in low light or behind cover. Mobile Surveillance Unit PTZ pulls in tight on the activity zone — most-vandalized corners, loading docks, rear walls, dumpster enclosures.

The SOC operator sees the live alert in seconds and initiates audio talk-down: "You are being recorded. Police have been dispatched. Leave the property now." This ends the attempt in the majority of cases before the spray, the rock, or the tool comes out. When it doesn't, plate capture and live video go to dispatched officers, and the incident package goes to your insurance and law enforcement contacts.

Repeat offender identification is part of the value. VDS preserves evidence across multiple incidents, builds a pattern file, and supports prosecution that breaks the cluster.

## Recommended VDS configuration

- **Mobile Surveillance Unit or Mobile Surveillance Unit at most-vandalized corners** — $2,200 or $1,500/mo. Site walk identifies the 2-3 highest-priority positions.
- **AI VisionStream rules** — loitering detection, after-hours zones, person-on-site, repeat-vehicle alerts.
- **24/7 US SOC** — audio talk-down, LE dispatch, insurance coordination, repeat offender pattern tracking.
- **Cloud VMS retention** — 30 days standard, 90+ days for evidence on active investigations.

A school with monthly graffiti incidents at $800 cleanup runs $9,600/year plus paint, plus staff time, plus parent complaints. A single Mobile Surveillance Unit at $18,000/year prevents the recurring damage, the cluster pattern, and the long-term reputational drift. Construction sites avoid much larger one-time hits — $10,000+ for sabotaged equipment is a single incident that pays for years of coverage.

## This is not the steady-state product

Most VDS deployments are 12-month or longer programs — a construction site through completion, an auto dealership year-round, a utility substation indefinitely. Tactical is the opposite use case: short-duration, time-critical, often unpredictable.

We built the tactical practice because customers kept calling us. A retail district had three smash-and-grab incidents in a week and needed cameras up by Friday. A municipality needed surge coverage after a homicide cleared an evidence radius. A utility had to redeploy crews and equipment to a substation after Hurricane Helene took out two of theirs.

The hardware is identical to our steady-state fleet. The operating model is different.

## What tactical deployments cover

### Post-incident surge coverage
A theft, vandalism, assault, or other documented incident has occurred. The customer needs visible deterrent and forensic coverage at the affected site within days, not weeks. Typical duration: 30-90 days, sometimes longer if criminal proceedings extend the evidence window.

### Severe weather and disaster response
